summary: This Informational report covers the IAB and W3C workshop on age-based restrictions on content access, held in October 2025. It summarizes the main discussion points and topics for further consideration. The views are the participants' and do not necessarily reflect those of the IAB or W3C.

eli5.summary: Experts met to discuss how websites might tell if someone is old enough to see something, and wrote down what they said.

questions: age based restrictions on content workshop
how to implement age restrictions online
subtitle: What experts learned about protecting children online through technical design.

tldr.problem: Governments worldwide are demanding that websites restrict access to young people, but the technical and architectural choices for implementing age-based restrictions are complex and involve difficult trade-offs between safety, privacy, and freedom.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB and W3C brought together technologists, policymakers, civil-society advocates, and business leaders for a three-day workshop to examine how the Internet could accommodate age-based access controls and identify the architectural implications.
tldr.outcome: The workshop concluded that no single technical solution can meet all requirements equally, and that sustained multi-stakeholder collaboration considering privacy, equity, and Internet openness is necessary to navigate this challenge responsibly.

today: This Informational report from October 2025 documents the workshop participants' views and discussion points, not a consensus position of the IAB or W3C. It is published for permanent record as a product of the IAB and serves as an input to ongoing policy discussions about age-based Internet access controls.

sections.title: Why This Workshop Happened
sections.content:
Around the world, regulators and lawmakers are pushing for mechanisms to restrict what young people can access on the Internet, trying to reduce potential harms. But implementing such restrictions technically is not straightforward. The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) and the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) convened a workshop in October 2025 to bring together technical experts, policy makers, civil-society organizations, and business leaders to discuss the nuances of technical and architectural choices involved in age-based restrictions.

The workshop was careful to focus on how such systems could work technically and architecturally, not on whether they should exist or what content should be restricted. Participants aimed to build a shared understanding of the properties, trade-offs, and implications of different proposed approaches.
sections.eli5: Different countries want websites to check if kids are old enough to see certain things. Experts got together to talk about how websites could do this fairly and safely.

sections.title: Four Key Roles
sections.content:
One of the most useful discussions identified four functional roles that any system for age-based restrictions must perform. Understanding these roles helps clarify where responsibility lies and what each actor needs to do.

The Verifier determines whether a person falls into a target age range. The Enforcer ensures that a person who does not satisfy the verifier cannot access restricted content or services. The Policy Selector determines which rules should apply based on the user's jurisdiction, status, or preferences. The Rater determines whether content requires age restrictions and what age ranges apply. Notably, a user's jurisdiction is often determined using IP geolocation mappings, though these have acknowledged accuracy limitations and can be circumvented with VPNs.
sections.eli5: There are four important jobs: someone checks your age, someone blocks you if you're too young, someone decides which rules apply where you live, and someone labels what content needs age checks.

sections.title: Age Assurance Methods
sections.content:
Workshop participants recognized the importance of establishing common vocabulary because participants often used different terms for the same concepts. Age assurance is an umbrella term for technology that provides information about someone's age, encompassing multiple specific methods. Age verification uses high assurance, often tied to official government documentation or digital credentials. Age estimation uses statistical processes, like facial age recognition, that produce probabilistic outputs.

Age inference draws on data sources (like email or phone records) to determine whether someone fits an age range. For example, evidence of online activity before a certain date might indicate someone is older than a threshold. Workshop discussions emphasized that no single technique is perfect. Age verification fails when people lack recognized credentials; age estimation produces false acceptances and rejections, with concerning accuracy biases against people with African ancestry; age inference can fail due to missing information.
sections.eli5: There are different ways to check age: asking for a government ID, using a computer program to guess someone's age from a photo, or looking at what someone did online in the past. Each way works sometimes but can fail or be unfair.

sections.title: Architectural Approaches and Trade-offs
sections.content:
The workshop explored three main deployment models for where age-based enforcement could happen. Service-based enforcement places the compliance burden on individual websites, creating friction from repeated verification flows and risking fragmentation. Network-based filtering, already used in some jurisdictions, offers broad coverage but limited accuracy and significant privacy costs. Device-based enforcement, where operating systems mediate access based on one-time verification, is praised for usability and consistency but criticized for concentrating power among major vendors.

A recurring theme was the reality of constraints. Laws often designate a single entity as responsible for effectiveness, and services naturally contract with specialist age-assurance providers because not every company can become expert in all verification techniques. The workshop recognized that multiple imperfect approaches combined are more likely to succeed than seeking a single perfect solution, acknowledging that any deployed system will be imperfect in some way.
sections.eli5: Websites could do age checks themselves, or your internet provider could filter for you, or your phone could control what you access. Each approach has good and bad sides, and using some combination might work better than picking just one.

sections.title: Privacy, Trust, and Broader Concerns
sections.content:
Privacy emerged as a central theme, though participants recognized that privacy concerns vary by context. When private information is used by actors in a proposed architecture, trust in those actors becomes critical. Workshop participants observed that users might have no prior knowledge of or trust in third-party providers contracted to verify age, and this situation might inadvertently train people to trust unfamiliar sites that request personal information.

Privacy-enhancing technologies like zero-knowledge proofs were discussed as promising tools, but participants noted they do not address circumvention risks, still introduce new information into the ecosystem, and are relatively untested. A key insight was that child safety requires far more than technical restrictions alone. The workshop emphasized that supporting children requires the cooperation of parents, guardians, educators, and services—not just access control. Restrictions are necessarily binary and lacking nuance, yet each child has unique needs, and the adults supporting them are best positioned to provide appropriate guidance.
sections.eli5: If companies know your age, they need to be trustworthy with that information. But keeping kids truly safe needs more than just blocking websites—it needs parents, teachers, and caring adults working together.
